# `gridmetrics`: the full metric grid {#sec-gridmetrics}

## What it does

`gridmetrics` is the workhorse of area-based forest inventory. For every
grid cell, it computes a large set of statistics from the heights and
intensities of the returns in that cell: height percentiles, mean and
variability, canopy cover, return counts, per-layer summaries, and
surface roughness. Models fit between these cell metrics and field plot
measurements (volume, biomass, basal area) are then applied to every cell
to map those attributes across a whole project area.

`gridmetrics` runs on one file, as here, or on a whole folder of tiles in
a batch mode that tiles, buffers, and processes them in parallel
(@sec-gridmetrics-batch). It also accepts a surface raster, such as a
photogrammetric surface model or a canopy height model, in place of a
point cloud (@sec-gridmetrics-surface). @sec-metrics defines every
metric.

## Example commands

{{< include ../examples/fragments/gridmetrics_commands.md >}}

## Options used

| Option | Value | What it does |
|:--------|:--------------------|:-------------------------|
| (second input) | `out/ground_dem.tif` | Ground surface, given as the second positional argument. `/ground:` works too. |
| `/cellsize` | `10` | Cell size, 10 ft. Match it to the size of your field plots when the grid will be used for plot-based models. |
| `/outdir` | `out/gridmetrics` | Folder for the raster, named `<input name>_gridmetrics.tif`. |
| `/strata` | `0.5,2,5,10,20` | Also summarize the returns in each of six height layers (@sec-densitymetrics). |
| `/strataraster` | | Write the per-layer summaries as raster bands, not only as table columns. |
| `/surfstats` | | Add `surface_area_ratio` and `roughness` bands computed from the highest return in each cell (@sec-gridsurfacestats). |
| `/output-table` | `out/gridmetrics/gridmetrics_table.csv` | Also write every metric as a CSV table, one row per cell. |

: Options used in the `gridmetrics` example. {#tbl-options-gridmetrics}

Options left at their defaults include `/minht:2` (returns below 2 ft
are left out of the height statistics), `/nodata:NA`, and `/noheight:0`
(@sec-conventions).

## Outputs

- **`TC_1372_forest200ft_gridmetrics.tif`**: one multiband GeoTIFF with
  176 named bands on this run. They include height statistics
  (`elev_min` to `elev_p99`, L-moments, and others), canopy cover and
  its variants (`canopy_cover`, `allcover`, `afcover`, and others),
  `point_density`, counts by return number (`r1count` to `r9count`),
  intensity statistics (`int_*`), `surface_area_ratio`, `roughness`, and
  seven bands per height layer (density, count, proportion, mean,
  standard deviation, minimum, maximum), plus six intensity bands per
  layer.
- **`gridmetrics_table.csv`**: one row per cell. It starts with the
  cell's column, row, and center coordinates (`Col`, `Row`, `X`, `Y`),
  its `TotalReturns` and `FirstReturns`, and `CanopyCover` and
  `PointDensity`, followed by the raster's metrics with the same names.
  The surface-roughness bands and the per-layer density bands are in the
  raster only.

`/output-mode:singleband` writes each metric as its own GeoTIFF instead.

## Results

@fig-gridmetrics-maps shows six representative bands, each on its own
scale. Maximum and 95th-percentile height follow the same crown pattern
as the canopy height model (@fig-canopymodel-maps) at a coarser cell
size. Canopy cover is high across this closed-canopy tile. Height
variability is highest where tall crowns sit next to gaps.

{{< include ../examples/fragments/gridmetrics_figures.md >}}

## Checks

@tbl-checks-gridmetrics confirms that the grid has the expected rows and
columns and sits on the tile, that no band is empty everywhere, that the
per-cell return counts match R, that no maximum height exceeds the
tallest point, and that the table has one row per cell and agrees with
the raster.

{{< include ../examples/fragments/gridmetrics_checks.md >}}

## Surface rasters as input {#sec-gridmetrics-surface}

### What it does

`gridmetrics` also accepts a surface raster in place of a point cloud:
a photogrammetric digital surface model (DSM) built from aerial imagery,
or a canopy height model from any source. This puts image-based and
model-based height sources through the same metrics as lidar, so they
can be compared cell for cell or used in the same plot models.

Each valid pixel counts as one return, placed at the pixel's centre.
Pixels holding the raster's nodata value are skipped. Given a ground
raster, a pixel's height is its surface value minus the ground elevation
at the pixel centre, interpolated from the four nearest ground cells;
pixels with no ground value underneath are skipped. Without a ground
raster, the pixel values are used as heights directly, which is right
for a canopy height model. The raster is read 512 rows at a time, so a
large raster is never held in memory all at once.

The example uses a different site from the rest of this manual: a
500 x 500 m area of a western Washington forest (the Grays Harbor site
in FUSION2-examples), in metres. The first run reads a 1 m surface model
built from WA State NAIP3D imagery and subtracts a 1 m USGS lidar ground
model. The second reads a 1 m canopy height model of the same area
predicted from imagery by Meta, with no ground raster.

### Example commands

{{< include ../examples/fragments/gridmetrics_surface_commands.md >}}

### Options used

| Option | Value | What it does |
|:--------|:--------------------|:-------------------------|
| (first input) | `naip3d_dsm.tif` | The surface raster. Band 1 is read. |
| (second input) | `usgs_lidar_dtm.tif` | Ground raster to subtract. Leave it out when the raster already holds heights above ground. |
| `/cellsize` | `20` | Cell size, 20 m. A whole multiple of the pixel size gives every cell the same number of pixels (400 here). |
| `/minht` | `2` | Pixels below 2 m are left out of the height statistics. |
| `/gpu` | | Enable CUDA GPU acceleration for DSM surface raster zonal metric calculations (computes 33-band zonal metrics in device memory, with automatic CPU fallback). |
| `/nogpu` | | Explicitly disable CUDA GPU acceleration and force CPU scanline execution. |
| `/profile` | | After the run, print how long each part of it took (@tbl-gridmetrics-profile). |

: Options used in the surface-raster example. {#tbl-options-gridmetrics-surface}

### GPU Acceleration

When compiled with CUDA support and executed on a system with a compatible NVIDIA GPU, `gridmetrics` supports GPU-accelerated zonal metric calculation for surface raster inputs (a DSM or canopy height model) via the `/gpu` switch:

1. **33-Band Zonal Engine**: Computes standard elevation percentiles, moments (mean, variance, skewness, kurtosis), L-moments, and canopy metrics directly on device memory across cell windows.
2. **Scanline Window Buffering**: Strips of pixel rows are uploaded to device memory and processed concurrently, keeping device memory footprint predictable regardless of raster width.
3. **Resilient Fallback**: If CUDA device allocation or initialization fails, `gridmetrics` logs an informational message and automatically falls back to multi-threaded CPU scanline processing. Point cloud inputs run via the multi-threaded CPU point cloud engine.
4. **Disabling Acceleration**: Use `/nogpu` to bypass CUDA checks and force CPU execution.

Every other single-file option works as it does for points, with three
differences. A raster has no intensity, so the `int_*` bands are left
out. Every pixel counts as a first return, so `FirstReturns` equals
`TotalReturns` and all pixels fall in `r1count`. `point_density` is
pixels per square unit, which reflects only the pixel size. Batch mode
(@sec-gridmetrics-batch) reads point files only, so surface rasters are
processed one file at a time.

### Outputs

- **`naip3d_dsm_gridmetrics.tif`** and **`meta_chm_gridmetrics.tif`**:
  one multiband GeoTIFF per run, named after the input raster, with 57
  bands. The grid starts at the raster's top-left corner and carries the
  raster's coordinate system.
- **`naip3d_dsm_table.csv`** and **`meta_chm_table.csv`**: the per-cell
  tables requested with `/output-table`.
- With `/profile`, a timing table printed to the console after the run.

### Results

@fig-gridmetrics-surface compares the 95th-percentile height from the
two sources. Both show the same tall stands. The Meta model reads lower
than the NAIP3D surface across most of the area, and close to zero in
the band of short vegetation across the middle, where the NAIP3D surface
shows several metres of height.

{{< include ../examples/fragments/gridmetrics_surface_figures.md >}}

@tbl-gridmetrics-profile shows the `/profile` timings for the NAIP3D
run. On a raster this small, writing the GeoTIFF and table takes most of
the time. On large inputs, the timings show whether reading the input,
assigning pixels or points to cells, computing metrics, or writing the
outputs is the step to speed up.

{{< include ../examples/fragments/gridmetrics_surface_profile.md >}}

### Checks

The reference values for these checks come from the `terra` R package:
the same pixel centres, the same ground raster sampled at each one, and
the heights grouped into the same 20 m cells. @tbl-checks-gridmetrics-surface
confirms that both grids cover the input raster with 25 x 25 cells, that
every cell holds the same number of pixels as in R, and that maximum and
mean height match R in every cell. They match within 0.01 m when the
ground is interpolated, and exactly for the canopy height model. The
check also confirms that the `/profile` table lists every part of the
run and that the parts add up to the total.

{{< include ../examples/fragments/gridmetrics_surface_checks.md >}}

## Batch mode on a folder of tiles {#sec-gridmetrics-batch}

### What it does

Given a folder instead of a file, `gridmetrics` treats every LAS/LAZ
file in it as one project. It divides the project area into processing
tiles, reads each tile's points plus a buffer of its neighbours' points,
computes the metrics for several tiles at once, and joins the tile
rasters into one virtual raster (`.vrt`). Each point is counted by
exactly one tile, so the buffer never doubles the returns along tile
edges. @sec-many-tiles compares batch mode with `pipeline`.

Without `/extent`, the project area is the input files' combined extent,
snapped outward to whole cells. With an `/extent` that no input file
overlaps, the run stops with an error that names where the files
actually are. The ground raster can be given as the second argument, as
in single-file mode, or with `/ground:`. A ground raster that cannot be
opened stops the run before any tile is processed.

The example runs batch mode on a folder holding the example tile, cut
into 100 ft tiles. Snapped outward to 10 ft cells, the tile's
200 x 200 ft area becomes 210 x 210 ft, so the run uses nine tiles. A
second command gives an `/extent` that misses the data.

### Example commands

{{< include ../examples/fragments/gridmetrics_batch_commands.md >}}

### Options used

| Option | Value | What it does |
|:--------|:--------------------|:-------------------------|
| (first input) | `out/gridmetrics_batch_input` | A folder of LAS/LAZ files. A folder, rather than a file, selects batch mode. |
| (second input) | `out/ground_dem.tif` | Ground raster. `/ground:` works too. |
| `/outdir` | `out/gridmetrics_batch` | Folder for the tile rasters, the virtual raster, and the log. |
| `/tilesize` | `100,100` | Processing tile width and height, 100 ft. |
| `/buffer` | `20` | Extra points read around each tile, 20 ft. |
| `/threads` | `2` | Number of tiles processed at once. |
| `/strata`, `/strataraster` | `0.5,2,5,10,20` | Per-layer summaries, written as raster bands as well as table columns. |
| `/output-table` | `.../gridmetrics_batch_table.csv` | Write each tile's table, then join them in tile order into this one table. |
| `/merge` | | Also copy the virtual raster into one GeoTIFF. |
| `/extent` | `0,0,1000,1000` | Second command only: an area that misses the data, which stops the run. |

: Options used in the batch-mode example. {#tbl-options-gridmetrics-batch}

### Outputs

- **`tile_0001.tif`** to **`tile_0009.tif`**, with a matching
  `tile_NNNN.csv` for each when `/output-table` is given: one multiband
  GeoTIFF per processing tile.
- **`project_gridmetrics.vrt`**: a virtual raster joining the tiles,
  with the same band names as the tile rasters (`elev_min`, `elev_max`,
  ...).
- **`project_gridmetrics_merged.tif`**: with `/merge`, the virtual raster
  copied into one GeoTIFF, with the same band names.
- **`gridmetrics_batch_table.csv`**: the joined table, one row per cell.
- **`gridmetrics_batch.log`**: the run's log.

### Results

@fig-gridmetrics-batch maps maximum height and the returns per cell from
the joined tiles. The return counts show no stripe along the tile
boundaries, which would appear if points in a tile's buffer were also
counted by that tile.

{{< include ../examples/fragments/gridmetrics_batch_figures.md >}}

### Checks

@tbl-checks-gridmetrics-batch confirms that the grid is the tile's
extent snapped to 10 ft cells, that the virtual raster and merged GeoTIFF
carry the tiles' band names, and that the returns summed over all cells
equal the tile's point count, cell by cell against R. It also confirms
that no maximum height exceeds the tallest point above ground, which
shows that the ground raster given as the second argument was
subtracted, and that the per-layer count bands add up to each cell's
returns. The second command must stop with a non-zero exit status and an
error message.

{{< include ../examples/fragments/gridmetrics_batch_checks.md >}}
